title: The leap
hook: the ocean to Lanka; Surasa's mouth; the mountain that offers rest

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting Rama: two disguises, and a monkey who knew his prince by how he spoke. Your line was you know your people. Now Hanuman remembers his strength, and the ocean is waiting. Day thirty-two.

Hanuman climbs a mountain on the shore, grows huge, and presses down so hard with his feet that the rocks crack and the trees shake loose their flowers. Then he jumps. The text makes a spectacle of it: blossoms from the trees pulled along behind him, his shadow racing over the waves like a ship. He's flying to Lanka, to find Sita. And halfway across, a mountain rises out of the sea. Its name is Mainaka. It speaks. It says: you're doing a great thing for a good cause. Rest on me. Eat some fruit. Catch your breath. It's a kind offer. It's a real mountain. And it's right there.
screen: `HE CRACKS THE MOUNTAIN.` → `HE JUMPS.` → `A MOUNTAIN RISES: REST ON ME.`

segments.voice: Hanuman thanks the mountain. He touches it with his hand, politely, so as not to be rude, and says: I've made a promise; I can't stop. And he flies on. That's the first test of the leap: a good thing that would slow you down. The second test comes straight after. The gods send Surasa, the mother of serpents, to see what he's made of. She rises out of the water with her mouth open and says: nobody passes me without going into my mouth. So Hanuman grows bigger. She opens her mouth wider. He grows bigger. Wider. It could go on forever. And then Hanuman does the clever thing. He shrinks, suddenly, to the size of a thumb, darts into her mouth and straight back out, and bows. I went in. Now let me go. Surasa laughs and blesses him. That's the second test: not everything is won by getting bigger. Sometimes you get small and quick. There's a third test after that, a shadow-grabbing creature, Simhika, and he defeats her too. All of this is in the fifth book of Valmiki's Ramayana, the Sundara Kanda, the beautiful book. It's the book about Hanuman, and many Hindus recite it whole, as a prayer, in hard times. Here's what the story knows. The leap isn't one jump. It's a hundred small choices in the air: say no to the comfortable rest, don't get into a size contest, keep going. The leap is the practice.
screen: `THANK THE MOUNTAIN. FLY ON.` · `SURASA'S MOUTH.` · `GET SMALL AND QUICK.` · `THE SUNDARA KANDA.` · then, large: `THE LEAP IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one leap you've been putting off. Sit and breathe. Name one thing you keep meaning to start. A call. A class. A hard conversation. Picture the mountain that keeps offering rest: later, not today, you've earned a break. Thank it, kindly, the way Hanuman did. Then picture the very first moment of the leap, just the first step. Breathe into that. The bell holds the time.
The leap. Hanuman flies the ocean to Lanka, declines the resting mountain, and slips through Surasa's mouth by getting small.
Your line: the leap is the practice. Today, take the first step of the thing you've put off, and say no to one comfortable rest. Day thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many Hindus read or recite the Sundara Kanda, the Ramayana's book of Hanuman's journey, as a devotional practice, sometimes in full over a day or across several days, especially in difficult times.

original.note: Sanskrit: the beautiful book, the fifth book of the Ramayana, about Hanuman's journey.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monkey jumps really far.
what it means: the leap is a string of choices: turn down the comfortable rest, don't get into a size contest, keep going.
what a scholar hears: the Sundara Kanda, the fifth book, is among the most recited parts of the Ramayana; why it's called beautiful is explained in several ways by tradition.

notes: Mainaka rises at the ocean's request to honor Hanuman; the script simplifies to 'a mountain rises out of the sea'. Confirm.
Surasa sent by the gods (and sages) to test him; thumb-size detail follows popular tellings of Sundara Kanda 1. Confirm.
Name 'Sundara Kanda': explanations vary (the beauty of the narrative, of Lanka, of Sita, or a childhood name of Hanuman). Script says tradition explains it several ways.
